The original proposed rulemaking issued in 2002 sought to create an exception to
the enhanced due diligence requirement for those offshore banks that were branches of
well-regulated foreign banks. Specifically, we proposed to exclude from enhanced due
diligence those foreign banks operating under an offshore banking license that are
branches of banks licensed in a jurisdiction where one or more banks had been
determined by the Federal Reserve to be subject to comprehensive supervision or
regulation on a consolidated basis. The notice of proposed rulemaking issued today takes
a different approach, focusing instead on clarifying that U.S. financial institutions have
some flexibility in applying the enhanced due diligence procedures on a risk-assessed
basis, tailoring the enhanced due diligence to the risks associated with the particular
account. Comments are sought on all aspects of this proposed rulemaking.
II. Private Banking Provisions
The final rule requires certain U.S. financial institutions to establish and maintain
a due diligence program for private banking accounts that is reasonably designed to
detect and report any known or suspected money laundering or suspicious activity.

encompasses a statement of principles of development as well as a code of conduct,
and outlines the ethical principles that must be adhered to, and promoted, by the
organisation and its members. Below is an excerpt from the Code related to
organisational integrity:
Governance

independent, active and informed governing body (e.g., the Board of

numeric.question: Compute the escalation rate of wires to any newly-added payee.
numeric.calculation:
1) Identify wires to newly-added payee Susan Harris: amounts in transactions[0..3] = 1,709.94; 3,891.95; 19,007.47; 72,405.35.
2) Compute escalation rate as last amount divided by first amount: 72,405.35 / 1,709.94 = 42.344...

statutory.question: Does the conduct described fall within 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) — Suspicious activity reporting requirements?
statutory.answer: Neutral: 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) suspicious activity reporting may be implicated, but the facts do not show that a covered financial institution detected the activity or had a statutory duty to file a SAR.
statutory.label: neutral
statutory.reasoning: 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) authorizes/mandates suspicious activity reporting by a “financial institution” (as defined under the BSA framework) when the institution detects facts that may indicate a violation of law or suspicious transactions, and it provides confidentiality/safe-harbor protections for such reports. Here, the fact pattern shows an individual customer (SYN_1a54a642) sending multiple wires to a newly added payee (Susan Harris) in amounts far exceeding the stated expected monthly volume, which could be “suspicious” in an AML sense. However, § 5318(g) applies to the reporting obligations of the financial institution, not to the customer’s conduct itself, and the facts do not identify (i) any specific covered financial institution involved, (ii) that the institution detected the suspicious activity, or (iii) that the institution failed to file (or did file) a report as required. Because those elements necessary to assess applicability of § 5318(g) suspicious activity reporting are not established, the statute’s application cannot be determined from the provided facts.
